title: Renaissance philosophy
wiki_lead: Renaissance philosophy encompasses the philosophical thought of the period corresponding to the Renaissance in Europe, running roughly from 1400 to 1600. It therefore overlaps both with late medieval philosophy, which in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries was influenced by notable figures such as Albert the Great, Thomas Aquinas, William of Ockham, and Marsilius of Padua, and early modern philosophy, which conventionally starts with René Descartes and his publication of the Discourse on Method in 1637.
wiki_excerpt:
Renaissance philosophy encompasses the philosophical thought of the period corresponding to the Renaissance in Europe, running roughly from 1400 to 1600. It therefore overlaps both with late medieval philosophy, which in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries was influenced by notable figures such as Albert the Great, Thomas Aquinas, William of Ockham, and Marsilius of Padua, and early modern philosophy, which conventionally starts with René Descartes and his publication of the Discourse on Method in 1637.


Continuities
The structure, sources, method, and topics of philosophy in the Renaissance had much in common with those of previous centuries.


Structure of philosophy
Particularly since the recovery of a great portion of Aristotelian writings in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, it became clear that, in addition to Aristotle's writings on logic, which had already been known, there were numerous others roughly having to do with natural philosophy, moral philosophy, and metaphysics. These areas provided the structure for the philosophy curriculum of the emerging universities. The general assumption was that the most 'scientific' branches of philosophy were those that were more theoretical and therefore more widely applicable. During the Renaissance too, many thinkers saw these as the main philosophical areas, with logic providing a training of the mind to approach the other three.


Sources of philosophy
A similar continuity can be seen in the case of sources. Although Aristotle was never an unquestioned authority (he was more often than not a springboard for discussion, and his opinions were often discussed along those of others, or the teaching of Holy Scripture), medieval lectures in physics consisted of reading Aristotle's Physics, lessons in moral philosophy consisted of examinations of his Nicomachean Ethics (and often his Politics), and metaphysics was approached through his Metaphysics. The assumption that Aristotle's works were foundational to an understanding of philosophy did not wane during the Renaissance, which saw a flourishing of new translations, commentaries, and other interpretations of his works, both in Latin and in the vernacular. After the Reformation, Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics continued to be the main authority for the discipline of ethics at Protestant universities until the late seventeenth century, with over fifty Protestant commentaries published on the Nicomachean Ethics before 1682.
In terms of method, philosophy was considered during the late Middle Ages as a subject that required robust enquiry on the part of people trained in the subject's technical vocabulary. Philosophical texts and problems were typically approached through university lectures and 'questions'. The latter, similar in some ways to modern debates, examined the pros and cons of particular philosophical positions or interpretations. They were one of the cornerstones of the 'scholastic method', made students who proposed or responded to questions quick on their feet, and required a deep familiarity with all of the known philosophical tradition, which would often be invoked in support of or against specific arguments. This style of philosophy continued to have a strong following in the Renaissance. Pico della Mirandola's Disputations, for instance, depended directly on this tradition, which was not at all limited to university lecture halls.


Topics in philosophy
Given the remarkable range of Aristotelian philosophy, it was possible to discuss all kinds of issues in medieval and Renaissance philosophy. Aristotle had treated directly problems such as the trajectory of missiles, the habits of animals, how knowledge is acquired, the freedom of the will, how virtue is connected with happiness, the relationship of the lunar and the sublunar worlds. grok_lead: Renaissance philosophy denotes the diverse philosophical inquiries and intellectual movements in Europe from the mid-14th to the late 17th century, driven by the rediscovery and translation of ancient Greek and Roman texts, which spurred a departure from medieval scholasticism toward renewed engagement with pagan antiquity and humanistic ideals. This era witnessed the recovery of lost works through interactions with Byzantine scholars and the fall of Constantinople in 1453, enabling direct access to primary sources that challenged the dominance of Aristotelian interpretations mediated by Arabic commentators. Central to its character was humanism, which prioritized the study of classical languages, rhetoric, and ethics to cultivate individual virtue and civic responsibility, often contrasting with the dialectical rigidity of scholastic theology. Prominent developments included the revival of Platonism under figures like Marsilio Ficino, who established the Platonic Academy in Florence and translated Plato's complete works into Latin, integrating them with Christian doctrine to emphasize metaphysical harmony between the divine intellect and human soul. In parallel, Aristotelian natural philosophy evolved through empirical observations and critiques, laying groundwork for later scientific methodologies, as seen in the works of Pietro Pomponazzi, who defended the eternity of the world against theological constraints using reason alone. Political realism emerged with NiccolÃ² Machiavelli's The Prince, advocating pragmatic power dynamics over moral idealism, reflecting causal analyses of state stability amid Italian city-state rivalries. Northern thinkers like Desiderius Erasmus advanced Christian humanism, critiquing ecclesiastical corruption through philological examination of scriptures, promoting irenicism and moral reform without dogmatic upheaval. These achievements fostered a pluralistic intellectual landscape, bridging antiquity and modernity by reconciling faith with reason, though tensions arose from Church condemnations of heterodox views, such as the Paduan Aristotelians' materialist leanings. Renaissance philosophy's legacy endures in the prioritization of textual fidelity, individual agency, and naturalistic explanations, influencing Enlightenment rationalism and empirical science, unencumbered by later ideological overlays that might obscure its roots in unvarnished classical recovery.
